_comment: Hand-authored survey data. Every cell carries its own evidence class and
citation; see README.md for what the classes mean. probe.py re-derives the
machine-checkable cells and prints what no longer matches. render.py turns
this file into survey.md -- do not edit survey.md.
A row is identified by its url, which is unique; vendor is not (Raspberry Pi has two rows) and neither was source before this was fixed.

evidence_classes.opened: the artefact was fetched here and its contents listed or read
evidence_classes.listed: the host's own file listing was read; the filenames are real, the files were not opened
evidence_classes.stated: a vendor page or README asserts it; nobody opened the artefact
evidence_classes.absent: a complete listing was searched and it is not there
evidence_classes.unreachable: the source could not be reached from here; what was tried is recorded

sources.model: per-kit versioned zip, eleven prior versions kept

licence.cite: License.txt inside the zip, 1,950 bytes, (c) 2010-2024 Nordic Semiconductor ASA

schematic_source.note: six Altium .SchDoc sheets (cover, nRF52840 MCU, interface MCU, misc, connectors, power supply) plus pca10056.PrjPCB and pca10056.IntLib

pcb_layout.note: 400236.PcbDoc, 15,106,048 bytes, plus a full Production files/ tree -- 14 gerber layers, 6 drill files, pick-and-place CSV, BOM .xls, assembly drawing and laminate spec

footprints_symbols.note: pca10056.IntLib, 4,599,808 bytes -- an Altium integrated library, so symbols and footprints together in a proprietary binary

notes: The conflict, recorded rather than resolved: the licence shipped with the hardware files says 'software' in every clause and forbids reverse-engineering anything supplied in binary form -- but what it is attached to is an Altium PCB project. Clause 4 further restricts use to designs built around a Nordic integrated circuit. Read literally it is a software licence stapled to a board design; read by intent it is a use grant limited to Nordic parts. Either reading rules out redistributing the files, so the practical answer is the same and the ambiguity does not need settling to act on it.

Completeness is the highest here of any vendor surveyed: schematic source, PCB source, gerbers, drill, BOM and pick-and-place, all in one download, and the flexible NFC antenna PCB as a second project alongside.

probe.py reports HTTP 403 for the download page and that is not a broken row: nordicsemi.com refuses non-browser clients on HEAD and on GET alike. The zip itself is served from nsscprodmedia.blob.core.windows.net and answers 200 -- which is where it was fetched from here.

notes: Six files in the sampled repository, and the whole board design is two of them. This is the tidiest per-board layout in the survey and the easiest to fetch selectively.

GitHub reports the licence as NOASSERTION because licence.txt is the CC-BY-SA 3.0 legal code rather than a recognised template. The README says only 'Creative Commons Attribution/Share-Alike' with no version, so the version is a fact about the file, not about the README.
634 repositories at roughly 1 MB each is the opposite shape from Seeed: nothing to fetch sparsely, but 634 things to enumerate.

Correction to this survey's first pass, which recorded EAGLE as 'proprietary binary' from the extension alone. EAGLE has written XML since version 6, so this row's schematic is machine-readable today. Three vendors were mis-recorded the same way and all three were opened to fix it -- which is precisely the failure the `opened` class exists to prevent, committed by the survey that defined it.

That is the specific reason a registry cannot store one licence per vendor: the failure mode is not a vendor changing its mind, it is a single repository missing a file.

Other hosts fetched successfully in the same minutes, so this is st.com from this network, not a general outage.
The Zephyr page reached fine and links ST's reference manual and UM2953 user manual, but no schematic -- so even the corroborating source does not confirm what ST publishes as CAD.

ST matters more than most rows here: docs/architectures.md picks STM32 C0/G0 as 'build our own' and names a $12 Nucleo-C031C6 as the oracle. The one vendor whose files this project most needs is the one row that could not be verified. Re-run probe.py from a network that can reach st.com before anyone builds on this.

notes: GitHub reports no licence for ch32v003, ch32v307, ch32v20x or ch32x035 -- the repositories that carry the hardware. Some siblings that do not (ch583, ch592, usb-jtag-spi) are Apache-2.0, which makes the omission look deliberate rather than forgotten.

The hardware is real Altium source and it is genuinely hard to find: buried under EVT/PUB/SCHPCB/ inside a repository that is mostly C headers and source, with 169 duplicated Eclipse project files per chip family. Nothing in the repository name or description says hardware is in there.
No licence on the repositories that matter, Apache-2.0 on ones that do not. Under those terms the files can be read but not redistributed, so this is a fetch-never-vendor source regardless of size.

board_support.note: pimoroni/pimoroni-pico, MIT, 10,597 KiB -- C++ and MicroPython libraries with pin definitions for their RP2040 boards, and no hardware artefacts of any kind

notes: Pimoroni publishes no board design files. Listed rather than omitted, because 'we checked and there is nothing' is the answer a registry needs; silence would read as 'not yet surveyed'.

What it does publish is component libraries and software, both openly. The only Pimoroni footprints anyone can use for a whole board are third-party -- there is a community KiCad footprint for the Tiny2040 and a forum thread asking for Yukon module footprints, which is what an absent vendor library looks like from the outside.
